Yes, for any commit that gets replayed. A commit's hash covers its tree, parent hash(es), author, committer, timestamp, and message. Rebasing changes the parent, so each replayed commit gets a new hash, and every descendant changes too, since each one's parent hash changed.

Commits below the new base, which aren't replayed, keep their hashes. If the rebase is a no-op (the branch is already on the target) or git fast-forwards, nothing changes. Commits that git drops because an identical patch is already upstream simply disappear.

That's why you shouldn't rebase commits others have already pulled: their copies keep the old hashes, so histories diverge.
